subtopic: MR. ASSELIN, NOTRE DAME DE GRACE-COMMENT IN MONTREAL "STAR" RESPECTING COURT PROCEEDINGS

speechtext:
Mr. Edmund Asselin (Notre Dame de
Grace): Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege affecting my honour and the rights and privileges of all Members of the House. The question of privilege arises from an article which appeared on the editorial page of the Montreal Star, Friday, May 28, 1965, entitled "The Asselin Judgment". The editorial refers to a judgment rendered May 25, 1965 by the Honourable Mr. Justice Paul Trepanier in a case before the Superior Court, Province of Quebec, district of Montreal, No. 660-374 and to a transaction which I had with the Protestant School Board of Montreal in 1960 and 1961, before I became a Member of the House of Commons. This editorial says that I am not fit to sit in this House because, and I quote from the article:
Mr. Asselin's dealings in this case were called into question by two inquiries.
Mr. Justice Paul Trepanier's judgment, while dismissing the action and assessing costs against the school board, rejects out of hand the allegation that I was in a position of trust or an agent or a mandator of the board, in these words-and I quote from the third paragraph of the judgment on page 12:
For the foregoing reasons the Court has come to the conclusion that the Plaintiff-
That is the school board.
-far from proving an express or a tacit mandate, has rather confirmed the allegations of the defence.
That is myself.
His Lordship deals with the other allegations in these terms. First I will quote from the last paragraph of page 12 of the judgment:
However, because of the publicity surrounding this matter and because of the allegation of subterfuge attributed to the Defendant and the obtaining of confidential information which might have a damaging effect on the reputation of the persons concerned in this matter who hold public offices the Court considers itself justified in glancing at these allegations.
Then at the bottom of page 13, after having rejected the allegations of subterfuge and having looked at the allegation of obtaining
confidential information, he rejects both, in these words:
Here again this allegation is absolutely contrary to the evidence.
His Lordship, in summing up in the fourth paragraph on page 14 of the judgment, goes much further; and I quote again:
On the whole, the Court has searched in vain for some motive to cast any blame whatsoever upon the Defendant or upon the officers of the Plaintiff-
That is the school board.
-in this whole transaction.
Mr. Speaker, if the Montreal Star's proposition were allowed to stand, then any Member of this House whose actions, even before he became a Member of this House, were called into question by an inquiry would ipso facto become unfit to sit in the House of Commons, even though the only basis or premise on which his actions were questioned was later declared by a properly constituted court to be unfounded and contrary to the evidence.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
If such were the case, Mr. Speaker, then any Member against whom unfounded accusations were levelled would be unfit to sit in this House, even though a judge of the Superior Court declared that there existed no impropriety and no reason to cast any blame whatsoever on that Member.
The Montreal Star's editorial denies the right to equality before and recourse to the courts for all Members of this House who have or who might be subjected to unfounded accusations, particularly with regard to their conduct as private citizens before being elected to this House.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: MR. COATES-REQUESTS FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER

subsubtopic: DIVISION OF FIELDS OF OPERATION BETWEEN TWO MAJOR CANADIAN AIR LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 24, 1964, I announced three principles which had been accepted by the Government as a basis for civil aviation policy. Since that time the main attention of the Government has been concentrated on working out the international aspect of civil aviation policy.
The first principle stated that, in the international field, air services provided by Canadian air lines should serve the Canadian

interest as a whole; that these services should not be competitive or conflicting, but should represent a single integrated plan, which could be achieved by amalgamation, by partnership or by a clear division of fields of operations.
In applying this principle, the Government decided to ask Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines to see whether they could agree themselves, after consultation, upon a basis for its application. The two air lines have agreed that the most effective way to carry out this policy would be by a clear division of their fields of operations so that outside Canada neither air line would serve any point served by the other. After considering many possible divisions of the world between the two air lines, it was finally concluded that the simplest approach would be to agree that each line should continue to serve all the points now served by it and that the geographical areas now served by each should be defined and extend so that practically the whole world be open to service by one air line or the other.
As a result, it has now been decided that Canadian Pacific Airlines will serve the whole Pacific area, the whole continent of Asia, Australia and New Zealand, southern and southeastern Europe and Latin America. Air Canada will serve the United Kingdom, western, northern and eastern Europe, and the Caribbean. The only exception to the clearcut division is that Canadian Pacific Airlines will continue to serve the Netherlands. This division accounts for the whole of the world except Africa and the United States. For the time being, neither air line is contemplating service to any part of Africa and the question of service to Africa will be left aside until some practical question arises. In the case of the United States, we continue to hope that negotations for a new bilateral will soon be completed. Once they have been completed a decision will be made as to which of the new points is to be served by each of our national air lines.
The Government has undertaken to regard Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines as its chosen instruments in the areas of the international operations allocated to each. The Government will pursue vigorously with the governments of other countries negotiations for extensions of Canadian service in their respective areas of operation. Negotiations have already been undertaken with several countries and as soon as these ne-
June 1, 1S65

gotiations are brought to a successful conclusion a further report will be made upon them.
Agreement has already been reached between the two carriers regarding sales and agency relationships. The agreement provides that in the international field each carrier is to represent the other to the best of its ability. The sales activities of both companies are on a basis of mutual assistance; sales personnel endeavour to meet the wishes of any customer by selling transportation over its own air line and, wherever feasible, over the other Canadian air line, so that passengers are encouraged to travel to their ultimate destinations by Canadian air lines. Other measures of co-operation between the two companies will be maintained. These include joint advice to the Government on bilateral air negotiations and joint servicing and support arrangements where appropriate.
The second principle announced on April 24, 1964, related to domestic main line services. In that announcement, competition was not rejected but the Government made it clear that any development of competition should not compromise or seriously injure the economic viability of Air Canada's main line domestic operations which represent the essential framework of its network of domestic services. In other words, it was stated that there must not be the kind of competition which would put Air Canada into the red; and, in the event that competition continued, the Air Transport Board should ensure an opportunity for growth to both lines above this basic minimum.
The Government has decided to employ a special aviation consultant to advise whether the growth of domestic main line service would now permit some further degree of competition on that basis and, if so, to recommend a suitable procedure for working out, from time to time, such extensions of service. Steps are being taken to secure the services of an outstanding international aviation consultant for this purpose.
The third principle announced on April 24, 1964 stated that a definition of the role for regional air carriers providing scheduled service was necessary, including a relationship with the main line carriers which would give the regional carriers a reasonable chance to operate without Governmental subsidies.
In the discussions with the Presidents of the two major air lines, it has been made clear that the Government expects them to take some responsibility to assist in working out that policy. There are many forms which such
Civil Aviation Policy
assistance might take, ranging through route transfers and route operations, contractual relations and various forms of technical and administrative support. Implementation of this co-operation is not something that will produce major results overnight, but it should have important results over a longer period.
The Presidents of the two major air lines as well as each of the major regional carriers are being requested to prepare special recommendations on measures by which they consider this third principle could be implemented; and on what specific steps could be taken by the major carriers, or by the Government, to improve the position of the principal regional air carriers. It is planned, in this connection, to arrange for continuing machinery of consultation and liaison between Air Canada, Canadian Pacific Airlines, the major regional carriers and the Government to ensure the development of adequate regional air carriers.
The development of Canadian civil aviation in accordance with these policies will provide for improved and more stable service for the Canadian public as well as a better economic framework for the carriers themselves. In the domestic field a degree of competition will remain to provide the public with the advantages that can result from a competitive atmosphere; while at the same time this policy will avoid the excesses of competition which were ruinous to all but one of the main railways of Canada in the past and which can result only in major added burdens for the taxpayer and, because of the inability of carriers to maintain heavy deficit positions, less satisfactory service to the public.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In the international field, competition with foreign carriers is already extremely keen and the joint approach by the two Canadian carriers will strengthen their position and provide better over-all service to the travelling public and a strengthening to Canada's position in world aviation.

I say at once that it would have been most helpful if the Opposition could have been furnished with a copy of the hon. gentleman's statement, which was apparently furnished to the press but denied to the Members of the House. It is a course of action that is not in keeping with the vociferous ideas to make Parliament effective, as the other side of the House would sometimes indicate is the purpose of the amendments to the processes of Parliament. No
181C

June 1, 19S5
Civil Aviation Policy
indication was given in advance that this matter would come up, and therefore it is quite impossible to deal with each and every matter referred to. Suffice it to say at the moment that this question will have to be looked into carefully on the basis of the statement made by the Minister. I believe that a day should be set aside for the consideration of this most important matter. Certainly, Parliament has had no opportunity to give any consideration to these matters.
In so far as international air lines are concerned, apparently the world is to be divided, where Canadian lines are concerned, between Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. On the face of it, that may or may not be fair and in keeping with the assurance that the very best possible service will be assured to Canadians who use these lines. As to domestic air lines, while giving voice support to competition, to the kind of competition that is near and dear to the hearts of high bureaucrats, we find that there is going to be competition, but the competition will be limited by the fact that no lines shall suffer and that competition will be competition if necessary, but not necessarily competition.
I believe this whole question should be brought before a Standing Committee of the House on railways and transportation in general, so that the whole question can be looked into. It is a plan that is made up of many various facets, and when you come to analyse it in the short time that has been available since the Minister started to speak it seems to be one of those plans designed to meet the immediate situation, but not having in it that security and definiteness that the future of aviation ought to have. If Canada is to gain a tremendous lead in the field of civil aviation, its policies should be clearly defined and understandable and at the same time available for the fullest discussion in the House of Commons. I hope that the matter will be brought before a Committee. Certainly, it is a plan that has all the earmarks of having been designated on the drawing board. Whether or not both presidents agreed is beside the question. So far as Canadian Pacific Airlines are concerned, they have to take what they are given.

Mr. Speaker, I would second the words of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). It would be very helpful if opposition spokesmen could have advance

copies of a complex policy statement such as we heard this afternoon.
I think if we are to have our two major air lines engaged in overseas business, it is well that there should be some agreement between them. At first glance it seems to me the division of the world is not quite equal and that C.P.A. has a much greater territory than Air Canada. In this connection I would be very much interested to see what traffic volumes there are in the divisions allocated to the air lines.
I believe the Minister said that on certain overseas routes C.P.A. would act as an instrument of Government policy. If this is the case, then I think all Members of the House would like to have the opportunity to question officials of C.P.A. in the Railways Committee, as they can now do with officials of Air Canada. If this company is to be acting for the Government in a certain capacity, then it should be open to question by hon. Members, and in the past we have not been able to do this.
Regarding domestic service, the Minister was not too specific concerning transcontinental runs. There is a suggestion that C.P.A. will receive more of the transcontinental routes than it has at present. I would remind him that for several years past, according to the testimony of the President of Air Canada, part of the losses suffered by that company were as a result of C.P.A. entering the transcontinental business. I hope we are not going to have a situation where competition is going to be allowed whether needed or not. We shall have to look into this very carefully.
Any remarks regarding regional air services we shall leave until there is a chance to study the Minister's statement in further detail.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I thank the right hon. gentleman for relieving my frustrations by not forgetting me. Second, I can answer at the moment the first part of his question in no better way, I think, than by quoting the way his own Government, very properly, answered through the then Solicitor General, Hon. J. W. Browne, who speaking for the Minister of Justice on February 26, 1962, in the House of Commons, had this to say, as reported at page 1245 of Hansard:
In accordance with long established policy I am declining to answer this question in the public interest. Questions such as this, and all others which have been asked regarding investigational procedures, could in due course, if answered, lead to disclosure of all methods which must necessarily be employed to protect the security of this country. Such revelations would be of great interest and value to groups within and outside Canada who have used conspiratorial methods to obtain Canadian information to which they are not entitled.
There should be no inference taken from my remarks and the form of my reply because such discussions, in whatever form they take, can only tend to imperil the difficult investigations which have to be carried out in the interests of our country. The policy of this government, and previous governments, has been to decline to answer such questions as not being in the interests of the public, and there is no intention of changing this policy.
I wish to make this statement as mine under my full responsibility.

maintopic: PROVISIONS FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, May 27, consideration of the motion as amended on May 27 of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Brewin:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business,
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1.	That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 30 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously rec-commended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting, interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(7)	No motion made by a Minister under Sections (5) and (6) of this Standing Order shall provide for the allocation of a period of time shorter than two days for the second reading, two days for the committee stage, and one day for the third reading of any bill. For the purposes of this section, third reading shall be deemed to have been considered for one day provided the order for third reading is called as the first item under Government Orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, if necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment cf the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that day, unless it is disposed of earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
(8)	During debate on any item of business or stage thereof for which an allocation of time has been made under this Standing Order, if an amend-

Mr. Speaker, before turning directly to the amendment of the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), I would like to comment briefly on the proposed provision which it would amend. In connection with the limitation of time for debate there is only one thing that seriously concerns me, and I think concerns many other Members, and in fact concerned the Members of the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization, namely the fear that some bad measure or poor legislation might be forced through the House before the Members of the Opposition, the press and news media of this country are able to arouse public opinion against it.
If we limit the time of debate as has been proposed in the resolution we are considering, even to the point where it has now been amended in that there would be roughly five days during which debate could not be closed off, it would still leave a comparatively short period of time during which some legislation that should not be passed, and which has not received sufficient public discussion, could be jammed through the House to the detriment of the Canadian people.
Experience has shown that following the introduction of a piece of legislation it occasionally takes a matter of weeks rather than days for the public to become fully aware of what is contained in it, particularly if there is something detrimental in it. How then can we gain time for public discussion without interminable debate in the House?
I think that the answer is not difficult.
I would suggest that we could provide a period of one week, on request, between
1830	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures each stage of a bill before it is adopted, and in the meantime the House could continue with other business. My proposal would be that on completion of the second reading of a bill, and on committee stage, 10 Members could request that the following stage of the bill be not proceeded with until one week hence. This would not enlarge the time of debate within the House but it would provide a period of time during which public discussion could be encouraged, and if the Opposition felt that public opinion was beginning to support it, then such measures could be pressed upon the Government as would encourage it to amend or withdraw the legislation.
If there were such a provision I would feel very much better about the limitation of time for debate. In proposing this suggestion at this time I am not going to propose an amendment. I am setting it forth for consideration, because at the conclusion of my remarks I intend to move a subamendment to that of the hon. Member for Greenwood, to put it in line with the remarks I made on Thursday night and to give some more equitable treatment to officers of the House. But in putting forward this proposal I would suggest that while the limitations that are in the resolution would be acceptable, the total time during which a piece of legislation could be before the public would be enlarged.
The result of my suggestion would be that it would take 21 days as a minimum from resolution stage to final passage, if there were continued opposition. There would still be no more time spent on debate, but it would permit the public, members of the press and the Opposition to give better consideration to a piece of legislation that undoubtedly would be controversial. It would result in proposed legislation taking up one day on the order paper, one day on resolution stage, two days on second reading, and elapsed period of seven days until committee stage, two days on committee stage, an elapsed period of seven days, and one day on third reading. This is a suggestion that would make the limitation of debate much more palatable and yet not abandon the principles we have already discussed.
It has also been suggested that the House could go into a debate without adjournment, which might achieve the same end in that it would draw public attention. I rather prefer the first suggestion, but at the moment I want to leave it at that.

On Thursday I briefly indicated my views on the amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Greenwood. Today I would like to take a little more time to develop my views and make some background comments on the whole question of time limitation.
During the past 10 years we have undergone a parliamentary development in what I call the decade of destruction. This parliamentary development came about of necessity, almost 10 years ago during the defence production debate and the pipe line debates of 1955-56. In fact it was on June 7, 1955, almost exactly 10 years ago, that second reading of the Defence Production Act was moved, and on July 7, 1955 the Government of the day made the first move to apply the guillotine, that the question be now put.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Reading the debates of that time, we can see how impossible it would have been for the Opposition meekly to accept the application of the rules as they then existed. Destruction, if I may call it such, was the only answer. The destruction thereby begun should have ended when it achieved its purpose; but unfortunately these practices, having succeeded in changing a government once in 1957, were carried forward into 1962 and 1963, again changing the government but with a great deal more destruction and much less success. We have moved into a period of destruction of accepted House procedures, of governments and of personalities.
I believe the public has become weary of this type of conduct. It has been exaggerated and blown up, we admit, but there is considerable foundation for the charges of continuing destruction from all quarters of this House. There are some who still believe that the only way to defeat a government is to destroy it. Over the past 10 years this has been the apparent development. It is my humble view, however, that it is equally important to provide an acceptable alternative to government as it is to destroy the one in existence. I do not believe that the people are prepared to vote for another party just because the one in power is terrible. Changes in the rules and procedures will not of themselves make any improvement in our efficiency, but the best indicator of the intentions of this House is a willingness to submit to some measure of self-discipline in the conduct of our affairs. That is why I am in favour in general, of the proposed changes in the rules as now constituted and in favour, also in general, of the time limitations pro-

posed by the hon. Member for Greenwood <Mr. Brewin).
I do not fear and have not feared restrictions on time for debate in this House if they are reasonable. Any Opposition worth its salt can jump the traces when the occasion requires; and that has happened. We already have closure and we already have the previous question in our rules. There is some reasonable doubt whether we need the amendments now being proposed, but in view of past history governments undoubtedly are unprepared to apply these two rules. If we are indicating to the people that we are now prepared to practice at least some self-discipline, then I am in favour of this proposal. Applying closure under another name, however, can never conceal the real intent.
I see in the efforts of the Special Committee, in this debate and in the willingness of the House in general to accept some limitations, some self-discipline, the beginning of an end to the decade of destruction that we have undergone. Some may ask, why end this destruction now and leave this terrible government in power when destruction was the only source of change at least twice in the past 10 years? The first thing I would say, of course, is that the government does not really need too much help in destruction; it is pretty good at self-destruction by reason of its own actions. Governments can be selfdestructive; they can be suicidal in their approach. I think in a situation like that it behooves every Member of the Opposition to help them, and to that extent I join in wholeheartedly. But I do not see any dangers to the Opposition at the present time in making a move toward the other alternative, that of providing an alternative government, rather than completely engrossing itself with destruction, not only of the government in power but the rules of the House, and Parliament itself which, whether rightly or wrongly, have come under very severe public scrutiny in the past few years.
If governments can be self-destructive, so can amendments. I think the hon. Member for Greenwood has permitted an otherwise good amendment to destroy itself by using it as the back door for something else. In this case he has brought in an otherwise good amendment to limit debate to 20 minutes on a bill that is the subject of a time limitation, and has spoiled it by also bringing in the principle of raising the standing of the leaders of the other Opposition parties and giving them a time equivalent to that of
House of Commons Procedures the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. I hope I am not considered unfair about this, Mr. Speaker, but the people have not seen fit to give the leaders of the other parties the standing or status for which they are asking under this particular amendment and in all fairness there is no reason why the House should give it to them either.
Conversely, if all five party leaders were given 40 minutes, I think the intention of the hon. Member for Greenwood would also be self-defeating. If each of them took his full time, it would certainly not shorten the discussion, so far as I am concerned, because we would have five 40-minute speeches right off the bat. Including this other proposal in the amendment is attempting to settle a major issue by the back door method, that major issue being the standing of the other three party leaders. I do not want to go into that subject now, Mr. Speaker, because it is not what we are discussing and it should not be part of the amendment at all. If the hon. Member wanted to put forward a responsible amendment-I agree with him that on such a debate we should be limited as to time, with certain exceptions-then he should not have destroyed it by bringing in another principle that we could discuss ad nauseam as we have done in the past and probably will in the future. While the time limitation is good, I would therefore have to vote against the whole amendment as it stands.

However, Mr. Speaker, the rules give us the right to sweeten an amendment that has been proposed and perhaps make it acceptable to all Members of the House. In this way we can perhaps accept an otherwise good amendment by eliminating the unacceptable and controversial portions of it. I think the general idea of limiting these debates to 20 minutes is good, but we do not want either to accept or discuss the other issue brought into this amendment. By way of amendment, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. Member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse):

Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to raise, very briefly, certain questions which have occurred to me with regard to the allocation of time and which relate to the amendment and subamendment that have been moved.
As I listened to the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) I thought that in introducing his amendment he was unnecessarily apologetic with regard to the importance of maintaining in this House the opportunity for every Member, whether he be from the back benches or the front benches, to speak on any subject coming before the House. This, of course, is a principle which relates to the very basic question of freedom of speech in the House. I think it has been nowhere better expressed than in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 117, which reads as follows:
(1) The privilege of freedom of speech enjoyed by members of Parliament is in truth the privilege of their constituents. It is secured to members not for their personal benefit, but to enable them to discharge the functions of their office without fear of prosecution, civil or criminal. The privileges of Parliament, as the Commons has declared in their protestations of 1621, are the birthright and inheritance of the subject. "Parliaments without parliamentary liberty, says Pym, are but a fair and plausible way into bondage. Freedom of debate being once foreclosed, the essence of the liberty of Parliament is withal dissolved".
I think all of us agree that some method must be found to ensure as a very practical matter that any Member who wishes to speak in this House should be able to do so. At the same time, all of us agree that there must be some procedure adopted so that it will be possible under appropriate circumstances for some limitation to be placed on debates.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I assume that the purpose of the amendment moved by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) is to assure a better opportunity for private Members to speak while limiting the length of time taken by each Member. The amendment moved by the hon. Member for Greenwood and the subamendment moved by the hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) in my view do not go far enough and would not achieve the purpose for which they were presumably intended.
It seems to me it is essential that when an order for the limitation of a debate is adopted, arrangements should be made so that the debate will go on until every Member has had an opportunity to speak even if that means
House of Commons Procedures the ordinary adjournment hour must be extended throughout the night.
Moreover, I feel that there can be a valid objection made against the suggestion put forward by the hon. Member for Greenwood on the grounds mentioned very briefly by the hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.
Sometimes I feel we have gone too far in the House in recognizing special rights and privileges on behalf of or pertaining to the Leaders of the smaller minority groups. We have in this House the position of Prime Minister and the position of Leader of the Official Opposition with respect to which special privileges are recognized, but there seems little point in encouraging the development of guerrilla bands of Parliamentarians by extending special privileges to the Leaders of the smaller groups. I suggest that the Leaders of the smaller groups really should not object to dispensing with these special privileges because presumably they feel that in due course of time their particular group will become the Official Opposition and eventually form the Government. There seems to be no reason why they should insist, while they are minority groups, on having the privileges which have in the past been reserved for the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Official Opposition.
I would go even further than that, Mr. Speaker. When an order limiting the time of a debate has been adopted, all hon. Members, including the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Official Opposition, should be in much the same position. Why should they have unlimited time, and why should not all Members of this House be treated the same when there has been a time limit put on the debate?
I realize that my suggestion has brought forth smiles from the knowledgeable Members on the other side. I would, however, suggest this to you, Mr. Speaker. We all recognize that it is much more difficult to say something worth while in a short speech than it is in a long speech. Brevity is very difficult to achieve. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and, indeed, the Leaders of the minority parties are quite confident of their ability to achieve brevity if necessary. Indeed, they have had more experience in speaking than most of us so there is even more reason why they should be subjected to the same discipline as the rest of us. All of us should be restricted

House of Commons Procedures as to time when a House order limiting the time permitted for debate has been adopted.
Having given some thought to these matters, I attempted to put my hand to the preparation of a subamendment, but it became so complicated I realized that the procedure we have been following in respect of paragraph 2 is really not the best possible procedure. We have been attempting to amend in this House provisions which are of vital importance to the functioning of Parliament and to the rights of Members. The debate has been interesting but I think that most people who have had anything to do with the drafting of important documents or provisions realize that the best results are not obtained when that drafting is done in the way which has been followed in this House during the last few days.
I thought the House Leader was very wise in adopting the suggestion that now appears in paragraph 1 to the effect that a special committee of the House be designated and instructed to work out the detailed changes in Standing Orders which would best achieve the principles which the House wishes to adopt. Instead of trying to draft and settle on the floor of this House the detailed wording of Standing Order 15-A relating to the allocation or limitation of time as set out in Standing Order 15-A, hon. Members might adopt the suggestion that the special committee be requested and instructed to work out the detailed changes in the Standing Orders which are necessary to give effect to the basic principles which the House accepts.
The two principles seem to me to be, first, that by appropriate procedure it should be possible for this House to limit the time of debate and, second, that the procedure must be such that any Member, no matter how recently elected to the House, should be able to rise in his or her place and speak on a measure. There are a number of ways by which this could be achieved. The length of time for speeches by individual Members should be shortened. Provision would have to be made for a time limit in respect of the total amount of time that can be used not only on the main motion but on various amendments. This is another matter not dealt with in the amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Greenwood. If Members were restricted to 20 minutes at a time and limited to a total of 30 or 40 minutes on the main motion and any amendments thereto this might be acceptable.
[Mr. Wahn.l

Another possibility which should be considered is the extension of the sitting time past the normal adjournment and throughout the night if necessary. I do not think that would be necessary very often but the fact that this rule existed would provide a guarantee to private Members.
In that regard I should like to mention that Members on the Government side of the House, and I refer to backbenchers, have a particular problem which does not affect other Members to the same extent. When we are negotiating to get on the speakers' list we are negotiating not only with friends and colleagues but also directly or indirectly with men who are important officers of the Crown; in other words, they are heads of the executive branch of Government. In principle I submit it is not sound for private Members on the Government side to have their rights to speak dependant upon negotiating arrangements with executive officers of the Crown.
In most cases we can anticipate that there would be no difficulty in this respect as a practical matter, but I submit to the House that it is unsound in principle and that this is an additional reason why private Members on this side of the House should insist upon the procedural rules being such as to guarantee and entrench the rights of private Members to speak during a debate, while at the same time permitting the debate to be restricted within reasonable limits.
Another possibility that might be considered by this Special Committee would be the right to yield the floor. In other words, if a Member is fortunate enough to get on the speakers' list and is allocated 20, 30 or 40 minutes, for example, he should have the right to yield to another Member of his party who wishes to say a few words.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This would mean that private negotiations could be carried on among members of a particular party so that if a Member could not get on the speakers' list he could make arrangements to be heard. This may or may not be a good idea but I think it should be considered. Another possibility would be for the available time to be allocated first of all among the political parties or groups on some appropriate basis. Then it could be divided later among the Members in those parties or groups who wished to speak. It seems to me this would be quite possible.
To entrench the right of any particular Member to speak it could be provided that
June 1, 1965

should a Member for some reason be unable to get on the list of speakers he could file his name with Mr. Speaker before the debate. Any extra time available would then be allocated among those Members who had filed their names with the Speaker either through the Whips or directly.
There are a number of other ways in which the two basic principles I have mentioned could be recognized but I think I have said enough to indicate that if we try to draft and amend Standing Order 15A on the floor of the House it is unlikely that the resulting order will be the best one possible. I believe this proposed Standing Order, dealing as it does with fundamental matters, should be most carefully drafted. Even after it has been drawn up by the Special Committee I assume it will be brought back to the House and an opportunity will be given for further amendment. At any rate the drafting would be done on a more businesslike basis than the basis on which it is being handled at the present time. The drafting of important documents is never settled in this way in other places, and the provision we are concerned with now is a most important one, indeed. It should be most carefully drafted and only then should it be presented to the House.
Before resuming my seat may I mention another subject. Representing as I do St. Paul's riding in Toronto, I would mention the fact that reference has been made to the possibility of appointing a permanent Speaker and reference has also been made to my riding in particular.

speechtext:
The other place is not a place which has any attraction for me. Reference has been made to the appointment of a permanent Speaker. I think it is natural that the question should be raised in connection with this order. I have known Hon. Roland Michener for a good many years. He is a good friend. I think the campaign we had in 1962 in St. Paul's riding was one of the most enjoyable events of my life. I have the greatest respect for him and I am sure he would make a competent Speaker.
At the same time I am inclined to agree with others that it is perhaps unfortunate that the names of particular individuals
House of Commons Procedures should have been introduced into this debate. I cannot believe this will assist in solving the problem that now faces us. Besides, I do not think all hon. Members will accept the suggestion that we should have as our Speaker a person who either in a formal or an informal way is, in effect, a Civil Service appointee. The Speaker should be one of us, freely elected, and he should have to run for re-election just as we have to do. Prom my personal experience let me say that any disadvantage which a Speaker suffers from having to be non-partisan and from having to be absent from his riding for long periods is in my view-my view may be a prejudiced one though I do not think so-outweighed by the prestige which he derives from his office.
Historically the Speaker was elected by the Members of the House of Commons to speak for them to the King, the chief executive officer in the state. By a process of historical evolution which is familiar to all of us and which is typically British, the chief executive officer is now the Prime Minister. Yet in practice the Speaker is nominated by the Prime Minister, his nomination being concurred in by the Leader of the Opposition. As a result we find ourselves in a situation where the chief executive officer of the Crown, the man who exercises all the great executive powers, nominates the Speaker of the House. This is a strange anomaly of our present system. It is true there is some protection inasmuch as the nomination is seconded by the Leader of the Opposition and approved by the House, but I think we could work out a procedure which would be more consistent with historical precedent and which wbuld ensure the continuance in office of an able Speaker without the necessity of establishing anything in the nature of a Civil Service appointee.
The institutions whose advantages we are now enjoying and which we are exercising when we speak in the House have come to us by inheritance but it is up to us to do our best to improve them. This whole discussion has brought up a tremendously important point which may not be entirely relevant, though goodness knows it is as relevant as the discussion of a permanent Speaker which seems to me to be totally irrelevant to this debate. This tremendously important point concerns the question of what is a recognized party. It seems to me that we have no right to interfere in any way with whatever parties want to exist in this country. We have no right to interfere with their appeals to the electorate.
If a party wants to run in every riding in Canada and lose four-fifths of its deposits, that is fine. It is free to do so. I am personally always upset when I hear people suggesting that somehow there is something bad about a multitude of parties running in elections. They have every right to do so, and if the major parties are not satisfying the Canadian public then it is quite appropriate that the smaller parties should run. However, I think we in this House have every right to determine, on the basis of the returns to the House, what is a recognized party, what constitutes a party for the purposes of Parliamentary procedure and operation. That is our business just as it is of those in any other assembly having more than two parties.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, perhaps this is not entirely relevant, but I could not accept the amendment, quite apart from the other reasons I have suggested, for the further reason that it uses the phrase that was used once before a year or two ago, "any recognized party", without any definition of what that is. Personally I say we as Members of Parliament have every right to decide what is a party.
I rather like the arrangements in the French National Assembly. There are 482 members in the French National Assembly and the rule there is that you have to have 30 members in order to be a recognized party, which is just a little over 6 per cent of the membership. That has produced, in the situation in France today, six recognized parties, and even if the other members of the Assembly-there are about 50 of them outside those six parties-group together they are not for parliamentary purposes a recognized party.

I think we really might well do something quite soon to define this for our own purposes. The figure of 6 per cent would perhaps be an acceptable one. Six per cent of 265 would be about 16. But whether you take 6, 5, 4, 3 or whatever per cent, having done this the Business Committee, when it is arranging the length of time of speeches, should quite rightly on second reading, but in my view nowhere else, give the two main officers of the House either an hour or possibly unlimited time.
It should give the Minister proposing a bill, the Member immediately responding to it, and the leaders of recognized parties, using that term in the sense I have spoken of, say 40 minutes or 30 minutes, with everyone else given such time as the nature of the legislation seems to require and as the various leaders work out in discussions together. In my view, at the committee stage, especially when one can speak more than once, the time allocation for everybody should not be more than 10 minutes.

In fact, they do not take the same risks as certain other corporations, and I am referring now to loan companies and finance companies, which take more risks than chartered banks. That is where again people in the low income brackets are to be pitied most. They are the ones who suffer most from the requirements of chartered banks when they want to borrow money and I remember many cases where people came to see me to explain their difficulties in borrowing from banks, because they were told, they did not have the necessary guarantees to meet the requirements of the banks. Mr. Speaker, we feel we have very good reasons to oppose the passing of this bill before the Bank Act is amended in such a way that the Canadian people will get more out of it.
You will understand from that that we hope the government will realize that it is piling up debts upon the Canadians of today and tomorrow and will wake up in time and really try to take a step in the right direction.
It is not practical therefore to adopt today a bill that would enable a group of people to obtain a new bank charter before we have changed our banking system to meet today's needs.
We find it very strange that some members use all the means at their disposal to prevent the passing of bills setting up provincial banks.
That happened to the province of Alberta a few years ago, and the same thing is being done this year with respect to the project of another province.
The financiers must be proud of their Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). He is a docile pupil and is quite well disposed toward them. He even goes as far as to say that the provinces have no business in the banking field. I presume that his masters will some day have an honorary degree bestowed upon him.
Coming back to this bill, I should like to add that the persons concerned with its passing would probably not be any worse than the others who already hold bank charters; however, we have no indication that they would be better either.
That would simply mean that new banks would be added to the already existing ones, thus spreading, within the limits of the legislation, the everlasting exploitation of the people.
I feel the grounds for the economic and financial confusion in which the Canadians find themselves just now, are not due to the fact that we have not enough banks; with the ones we have, this country has succeeded in running into debt to the extent that some Finance ministers are unable to state precisely to whom we owe money, and hardly succeed in paying the interest on our ever increasing astronomical debts.
On the basis that banks create money and contribute to the piling up of debts, I see 22620-118
Private Bills
no reason to hurry and adopt this bill which would enable a new bank to make us pile up more debts. I wish to clearly define our attitude toward the usefulness of Canadian banking organizations in so far as they are concerned with the handling of money to facilitate the exchange of goods. We are in full agreement in recognizing the usefulness of banking institutions, and I am happy to add that all bank employees enjoy a well-deserved reputation of honesty in fulfilling their respective duties as responsible stewards of their firms.
Being aware of the important part that our banking institutions could play, the Credi-tistes have never thought of nationalizing the banking system. We recognize that free enterprise, with proper leadership, has a greater opportunity to play an effective role for the population in all spheres of activity.
What is essential and unfortunately not understood well enough in the operation of the administrative structure of the banking system is that the true assets of the banks are not represented by something tangible. The true assets of the banks lie in the difference between the total amount of real money in circulation and the total amount of bank credit, not only the credit which truly exists, but also the potential credit which remains as such through the will of the masters of the financial system.
Nowadays, money is created within the banking system through the granting of loans. Such loans are made mostly under the form of entries in bank books to the credit of the borrower. The loan creates a new credit which did not exist before; that credit has all the properties of cash: it is put in circulation by cheques issued by the borrower to make payments.
It is withdrawn from circulation through sales of products or through corporation taxes and then returned to the bank for wiping off.
If the ratio and the amount of loans are higher than the ratio and the amount of reimbursements, there is an expansion of credit, and, therefore, of the the money in circulation.
On the other hand, if the ratio and the amount of reimbursements are higher than the ratio and the amount of loans, there is a decrease in the circulation of the money. Such a decrease may be caused by more severe conditions imposed upon borrowers, by an increase in the interest rates or by a straight refusal of loans. That is what we call the restriction of financial credit, which is the main form of modern money.

Therefore, financial credit depends upon the central or commercial banks.
Whereas real credit is a social credit, financial credit is a bank credit. There is no financial credit possible without real credit. Money to pay the producers and what they produce would be useless if there were no producers and no production.
The people who create money, the bankers, determine the country's money supply. When they make some and let it circulate, everything is fine. But when they force people to bring back to the bank ah the money they created, things take a turn for the worse. When things go badly, when nothing is being sold and unemployment is on the increase, this is called a depression. A depression is a lack of money. I would like the party politicians to tell us what was missing from 1929 to 1939, besides money.
Since that period which showed up the system's absurdity, our politicians have been looking for other words to describe a period of inactivity. Those crises were called recessions, depressions or described by other terms changing nothing to the demoralizing effect of that stagnation of the monetary service, because crises, stagnation or recessions are due to the money system which is badly managed.
That great American industrialist, Henry Ford, was quite right in saying that if the public knew how money was issued they would not tolerate the system 24 hours.
It would be good to think over these things from time to time in view of the difficulties with which we have been faced in Canada for so long.
Why should a sovereign government, as this Canadian government, borrow from a chartered bank in order to foster the prosperity of the country?
Why must the Canadian government, which has the exclusive legal powers on our money, pay interest on money borrowed from the chartered banks, and then turn around and levy taxes to pay that interest?
Why must all our money in circulation bear interest when it is a well-known fact that the government is empowered to use other methods so that there will always be sufficient funds to meet this need?
Those many questions require consideration and our opponents have always refused to discuss them except to poke fun at them. This was not the case, however, with Mr. Graham Towers when he appeared before the

committee on banking and commerce in 1939. Thus on page 409 of Proceedings and Evidence, it is interesting to note his answer to the following question:
Could you tell me why a government empowered to create money hands over this power to a private monopoly and then borrows what parliament can create itself and on which it pays interest to the point of leading the country to bankruptcy?
Here is the answer:
We realize that the payment undoubtedly serves to pay off part of the operating costs of banks and a certain amount of interest on deposits. Now, if parliament wants to change the method of operation of the banking system, it is surely empowered to do so.
We, Creditistes, would like to know why governments, both Liberal and Conservative, have always refused in the past to amend the Bank Act so as to provide that parliament should issue at least part of the currency needed by the country.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
There is no doubt that our present system has become a dictatorship. The whole economic life depends on its decisions. Today money is in fact only a bookkeeping arrangement; it would be quite easy to make the bookkeeping fit the reality.
We notice that as a country develops, it gets deeper and deeper into debt with the financial interests who do not even grow a sheaf of wheat. I am inclined to think that the main reasons which prevent people from giving sufficient thought to that matter is the fact that no one tries to see the fundamental difference between true wealth and its symbol. Too much emphasis is placed on money, whereas commodities and goods are the true wealth. When one talks of wheat, butter, cheese, eggs, shoes, clothing, houses, that is the real wealth. We talk about real things, of things capable of satisfying human material needs such as food, clothing and shelter.
To talk about dollars, pounds sterling, francs, is to speak of symbols, financial symbols. Those symbols cannot by themselves provide food, clothing, shelter, and medical care. They are mere symbols, symbols created to assess the value of things and also, in our organized world, to give to their bearers the right to get things of their choice.
We agree on that point. But the more important of the two is, of course, the real thing. Without the real thing, without production, without the thing, the symbol would be meaningless. Put a hungry man in a desert with a roll of bills in his hand; he will die of
June 1, 1965

hunger. Bread would be much better for him. And if, in a city, a man with a roll of bills does not die of hunger, it is because he is careful to exchange his dollars for food.
Reality depends upon the production capacity of a country; its natural resources, its soil, its climate, its manpower and its brains, its machinery, its production processes, its work repartition, its social order, etc.
This productive capacity of the country, effective or potential, is the very basis of the confidence of its inhabitants or of those who come to settle there. Even before it was put to work, this potential capacity of our country gave some French people enough confidence for them to leave their mother country and come to settle on the shores of the St. Lawrence.
Today, the Canadian production system, while it has not reached its full potentialities, does not worry anyone. There is not a single Canadian who fears that, say, within 10 or 50 years, this country will be unable to produce wheat, meat, timber, or manufactured goods. There is unrestricted confidence in the production system of Canada.
If the financial system were the exact replica of the production system, it would inspire exactly the same confidence as the latter. Such is not the case, however. If nobody is apprehensive about Canadian production, many Canadians have fears concerning their financial capacity to obtain products.
Indeed, there is sustained progress in the production system, but the financial system is subject to continuous disorders. Symbols bear no exact and constant relation with things.
Dollars are plentiful in time of war when the production system is diverted toward things that do not meet at all individual needs. When the production system is the more capable of providing all that is being asked of it, the dollars needed to give orders vanish.
That is not only antisocial, but inhuman. Because of that, consumers are deprived while production goes unused. When there are hundreds of thousands unemployed, it means that goods are not being produced. If we have unemployed, it is because the governments, through their budgets are unable to put them to work. It is absurd but, unfortunately, that is the situation which prevails. As I said that is inhuman because consumers are suffering even though goods go unused. That creates artificial problems not only for individuals but for groups and even governments.

Consquently, it is not exaggerated to say that nine tenths of the problems are financial. When federal and provincial leaders meet in order to reach agreements, they always argue about financial questions. They do not disagree on means to develop agriculture, mining and transportation, but on the right to tax such and such a field. Those hon. gentlemen are doing their utmost to obtain the privilege of taxing their fellow citizens. It is a question of money.
If products are the only real wealth and if financing is but a question of dollars the dollar sign becomes more and more important because the law requires that money be given in exchange for things we cannot produce ourselves.
Bread is the staff of life, but if you do not make your own bread yourself, you can only get some if you have money. The importance of the dollar is such that you cannot obtain bread without it.
This is a very important matter nowdays because in order to live everybody needs things produced by other persons. Therefore, this symbol, the dollar, is really a lease on life. It you have this lease you can get what you want out of a producer system; but if it is lacking that is the dollar, you get nothing and the producer system bogs down instead of serving you.
Thus, control over money and credit means control over the life of the individuals. This control is in the hands of a few individuals who determine the creation of money, conditions under which it will be put into circulation and how long it will remain in circulation.
They wield a sovereign power without assuming the responsibilities.
That is a serious situation, and I think it is worthwhile to pause in order to take a serious look at the decisions that are taken and which have a tremendous impact on the future of the nation. The question is not whether that system would be harmful at the international level or whether it would place us in a situation where we might have problems-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks in

June 1, 1965

support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) to give a six months' hoist to that well known project for the setting up of a new bank in order to give the house the opportunity to take a new look at the banking reforms that were proposed.
Mr. Speaker, I am always amazed at the eagerness displayed by some hon. members in trying to force something on us against our will. What would it mean for the government to postpone that discussion for two or three months, so that we could carry out the job that is a compelling necessity at the present time, namely the revision of our banking system? Then, we could decide about accepting or turning down the applications to increase the number of banks in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, a Conservative member asked a while ago whether we wanted to kill this bill for the setting up of a new chartered bank. I have said and repeated in this House that we are not against chartered banks. On the contrary, we are in favour of the chartered banks which are a part of our financial system, but we are for chartered banks which play their true role within our financial system. We want to give back to chartered banks their true role. Actually, we contend that they play part of the role which is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada, while the latter remains idle and is well satisfied to entrust the task to the chartered banks, private institutions which take possession of the public wealth. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, with $8, and soon with $7, the chartered banks will be able to lend $100. With only a $7 deposit at the Bank of Canada, they will be able to lend $100.
Mr. Speaker, under such conditions, we would all like to have our own little bank; for myself, as a tradesman, I can assure you that if money I have on deposit at the bank could be multiplied in this way, I would do a terrific business within a year.
And the people cannot understand that. I do not know whether it is because the whole house has become a minion of this banking system which, year after year, grabs the wealth of our country, because the more an individual works, the poorer he gets and the deeper he gets into debt.
But where is all this taking us? As the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) pointed out a moment ago, we are heading toward bankruptcy, and at 75 miles an hour, if we do not wake up and put things back in order in our financial system, in short, if we do not hand over the part played by the chartered banks-which belong to the private

sector and not to that of the general public- to the Bank of Canada, if we do not compel the Bank of Canada to assume its role in the large public sector. There is no question about that.
It seems to me that if all members of this house wanted to make some effort to study and get to know the situation, they would finally understand. I realize that there are a few who know something but cannot talk. They cannot talk because, as they say themselves, it is very dangerous to speak of those things. It is a mystery that has never been explained to us from the day we were born, even from the day our great grandfathers were born, that the financial system could grab the output of the work of all the people throughout the country, because after all what is the financial system? Surely it is not a question of dollars and cents. As a matter of fact, I could simply compare the present financial system to a bookkeeping system. The Bank of Canada is simply asked to keep the accounts of the country, just as a manufacturer keeps his own books. If you want to make a better comparison, you just have to bring down this bookkeeping to the family level.
As a matter of fact, a family head works for a whole year and uses part of his savings to support his family, to improve his property and, at the end of the year, if he has $1,500 or $2,000 left, what he is going to do with it? Is he going to call on his neighbor and say: "Now take those $2,000, I have just created this amount, it is a net profit. If I need it, I will borrow it from you". If he did, he would undoubtedly be called an idiot. Nevertheless, this is how the assets of the country are administered. The Bank of Canada should be responsible for the bookkeeping of this country. Every year, a gain is realized since everybody is working. If every Canadian stopped working, then there would not be any gain.
Every year a gain of $10, $12 and even $13 billion is announced after balancing our earnings against our expenditures. This is a bookkeeping entry. But if a credit of $8 billion appears at the bottom of the column, the Bank of Canada is asked to do a bit of work and enter this amount to the credit of the country.
Therefore, if one has a $10 billion credit and needs $50 million in order to build a bridge, or if a province is in need of money, it should be taken out of the new accounting credits of the country, in the same way as an individual who has a $2,000 deposit in the bank
June 1, 18S5

and needs $50 in order to buy medicine for his wife. What will he do then? He is not going to borrow $50, but will take that amount out of the $2,000 he has. He will not pay any interest either, because he is not going to pay interest to himself on his own money. It belongs to him. The same applies to the country which is a great big family. It is merely the country's bookkeeping and, at the end of the year, a credit of $10, $12 or $13 billion is shown, which constitutes the annual gains, the outcome of the Canadian people's work, as indicated by a figure.

I would emphasize, therefore, that, obviously not in this particular debate but very soon if we do not want to be in quite serious trouble in this House, we should try to secure a definition of "party" for parliamentary purposes comparable to the one in say the French National Assembly.

It seems to me we must decide very soon what we mean by a representative party.

speechtext: What do you do with independents?

maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
