speechtext:
Exactly what they do with them in France. As I said before, in France there are 482 members. About 432 of those members belong to six parties having more than 30 members apiece. The smallest party has 32. The remaining 50 odd may belong to a party which is not recognized as a party in the parliamentary sense, but they still represent their constituencies and have opportunities to speak. They are still given
June 1. 1965

House of Commons Procedures all the rights of individual members of parliament but not the rights of members of parties in parliament, even though they may belong to parties outside. In France the situation at the moment is that approximately 432 of the 482 members belong to six parties, the smallest having 32 members. The minimum allowed is 30 members. The remaining 50 members of parties with less than 30 are members but even though they belong to a party outside the chamber they are, as I say, not recognized inside the chamber as a party.
Finally, may I say that I think the debate on this resolution, part of which I have heard and the rest of which I have read, has been extremely interesting and valuable. Part of its value, and a very large part in my view anyway, is derived from the fact that there was a fairly close examination of all these problems by the Committee on Procedure. This has convinced me that there is much to be said about committees of the House threshing through problems in order to try to reach agreement and canvassing a lot of opinions even before the Government of the day brings down a resolution of this sort. My hope is that this will set a precedent and that we shall do this at other times. I am sure that we would not have had this debate had not the Government canvassed the ground pretty thoroughly in the first place.

maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in agreement with the last speaker when she said that this has been a fairly interesting debate. I am sure that if I were in a mood to be very charitable I might find in some of her other remarks something with which I could agree. For instance, on the question of the recognition of smaller parties and their having a certain percentage of the membership of the House, I thought she was a little generous when she suggested 6 per cent as in France. I would put the figure higher here.
However, my purpose in joining in the debate is not to quibble about what sort of reforms should take place but really to express my puzzlement over why the debate should have taken this form. Frankly, I have not been convinced that we need this overhaul of the rules of Parliament. Speaker after speaker has risen to his or her feet and said that obviously we are in disgrace, that the public thinks this and that and that therefore the rules need reforming. This reminds me of a hockey game; if it is a bad hockey game then you must change the rules of hockey,

or perhaps the trouble is just a couple of bad teams. If there is something wrong with your car then you decide that automobiles are no good, that you should switch to tractors if there is something wrong with your automobile. It seems to me that just because the House or because Parliament does not have a particularly good reputation at a certain time it does not mean there is anything necessarily wrong with the rules. It may be a failure to observe the rules. It may be a failure of the House to organize its work. It may be that certain members have sabotaged the work of the House. There are a hundred and one ways in which Parliament can get a bad name, none of which should necessarily mean revising the rules.
Therefore I should have thought, after all the time spent on this debate, that someone would have spent some time explaining to us why it is that the rules of the House are at fault and not the particular make-up of the House. For instance, no one has spent much time pointing out that we now have five parties and what the effect of that is when normally we expect only two or three parties. No one has bothered to mention the minority position. Very few have bothered to explain why it is that we are now so insistent on changing the rules when everybody recognizes that any body such as Parliament can function only as well as the leadership which it is given. Parliament today has received the least leadership it has ever received. Therefore it seems incongruous to me that we should spend all our time talking about reforming and changing our rules when nobody has bothered to prove that changes in our rules are necessary.
I think most hon. Members must have been absent or asleep or just have not bothered to look at the speech made last Tuesday by, for instance, the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), which is to be found at page 1641 of Hansard, during which he talked about the functions of Parliament, what it is supposed to do and how it is supposed to do it. How can Members blithely stand up and so carelessly, I think, talk about limiting speeches and by how much they should be limited while at the same time ignoring completely the duty not just of the House in general but of every Member of the House to scrutinize closely Government spending? What has democracy come to and what do we think of Parliament today? I suppose we are just a rubber stamp and that the idea of streamlining the rules is that we shall become a more efficient rubber stamp.
June 1, 1965	COMMONS
Can any Member of this House contend that it is not necessary to consider whether it is desirable to change our rules, that there is no question about it, that it is self-evident? If they were to look at the conduct of this House and the leadership which it had last year, they would soon discover whether it was the rules that were to blame or whether it was something else. If we examined the situation and found that other things were to blame, would we still insist that the only purpose of this debate is to change our rules? How short are our memories? How much we have forgotten what happened to Parliament in the last session? We in this House are politicians, and we understand how little leadership we have received. We understand the propaganda put forth by the Government and why they bend all their efforts to make sure that no one in this country should blame the Government's lack of leadership for the trouble with Parliament. Yet it is the Grits who have the effrontery to say to the people of this country that Parliament is at fault, that the rules should be changed, if not us.
I remember, Mr. Speaker, some of the difficulties we encountered when the Government made that great change in the Department of Agriculture by order in council by means of which they switched five branches of the Department to the Department of Forestry and did not bother to publicize the fact. Then three weeks later they cancelled it. They did not switch them back but cancelled the order. Then two or three weeks after that they passed another order in council and transferred three more. Then we started to ask questions about it. Where were we in the interval? What was the position? Was it legal?
Here is a case where Members must ask themselves whether we need a change in the rules to discover why Parliament could not get these answers or why we spent so much time trying to find out the legality of the position. Between February and April we asked questions day after day but got no answers. Certainly it is the business of Members of Parliament to make sure that when public moneys are spent they are spent legally. But when a Member of Parliament telephones a Department and asks whether ARDA is in the Department of Forestry or the Department of Agriculture and the people in ARDA do not even know the answer themselves, is that the sort of situation about which Members of Parliament should be concerned? I would suggest, in the light of the thinking of the Government in these reforms, 22620-119
DEBATES	1851
House of Commons Procedures that after two or three weeks of asking questions about the situation and hammering away we would have been cut off. It would not matter whether or not the people of Canada had been given the answers. We would be told that the time provided had been sufficient.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Is there a Member of this House who does not believe in his heart that not only is it the business of the Government to run the country but the business of the Government to give leadership to this House and to make sure that our business is properly carried out? Most people believe that the Government must run the business of this country in a proper manner and must at the same time satisfy the Members of this House that they know what they are doing and that it is being done right.
Surely this is the place where we must force the Government to prove to the people of this country that the business of this country is carried out properly. How can we do that if we choke off the Opposition and allow the Government to deceive the people as to where the fault lies for an improperly run Parliament? This can happen when the Government is successful in selling to the people of this country that great bogeyman that Parliament is being obstructed by an Opposition which will not co-operate but insists on filibustering. Since when has it not been part of the Government's job to handle properly the House of Commons? Since when can those individuals on the front benches of the Government side say with propriety in their petty way that they cannot lead Parliament and the Government because of the Opposition, and that the people of Canada should help to throttle the Opposition? That is a preposterous situation.
Do we hear often those on the Government benches arguing to sustain the request that we amend the rules in order to throttle the Opposition? The obvious answer to that question is no. It seems that someone has taken it for granted that because the press has suggested that Parliament is not working efficiently the rules are at fault. Many Members of this House seem to have accepted that conclusion. I am not one of those who go along with the mob, and perhaps I am wrong in this regard. It may be that the rules are at fault, but when I consider the many other things that in my opinion are at least partially responsible for the inefficiency of Parliament I am inclined to look elsewhere.
June 1, 1965

House of Commons Procedures
For instance, I must consider the lack of leadership on the part of the Government and the contempt this Government has shown in so many ways for Parliament itself. There are many solid and substantive reasons why Parliament has not been able to carry out the important business of this country in the way each one of us would like to see it carried out. For these and other reasons I have become suspicious about the suggestion that the blame can be laid at the doorstep of the rules and that the situation can be solved by a change thereof.
An institution such as this House of Commons, which has existed for many years in good times and in bad with minority Governments and majority Governments, and which has by and large done a creditable job, must have rules which are not all bad. This institution has by and large for a number of years managed to retain public confidence in its ability to do the job of Government, and I am a little suspicious now about the sudden desire to change the rules.
Perhaps in this age people find things too easy. Perhaps they are uneasy about the atomic bomb and want to find a quick and easy shelter. With a Government as weak as the Government we now have, I am not surprised that the people are scurrying as fast as possible behind a quick and easy solution to the problem.

maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext: Would the hon. Member permit a question?

maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
When I have completed my speech I shall be pleased to entertain questions. I understand the position taken by the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), and I will comment on that position in a moment or two.
Having regard to the number of things which influence the efficiency or otherwise of Parliament, the difficulty with which we are now faced may relate to our rules and perhaps we should change them, but before agreeing to do so let us consider a number of other things which may also be at fault. The hon. Member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) today, on a question of privilege, referred to the laxity on the part of the Government in replying to questions. We all know how much difficulty the Speaker has in trying to keep the Members in line in respect of questions and how often he has suggested that questions be placed on the order paper. We also know the number of times hon. Mem-

bers have complained because, having placed questions on the order paper, the information has not been forthcoming. I suggest this is another indication of the lack of leadership on the part of the Government and the lack of respect it has for Parliament and the operation of the parliamentary system.
The present Government apparently regards Parliament as a nuisance. Many of us remember the pipe line debate and how it came about. We remember well the people on the Government side involved in that debate and their lack at that time of respect for Parliament. I also have some reason to remember Easter of last year. A number of Members on the other side of this House feel that my complaint resulted in our not having an Easter recess. At that time we asked for certain answers and gave the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) notice a week ahead that unless we received the information requested we would not give unanimous consent to the motion to adjourn for an Easter recess. The Government at that time had so little regard for Parliament it thought that it could steamroll certain things through the House under the threat that unless we agreed we would have no recess.
Let us remember the time we found that the Government was concealing the condition of the unemployment insurance fund. I remember those hon. Members squirming, when we were in power, as a result of information we brought forward. I remember how embarrassed the hon. Member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and the hon. Member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) were in this regard. I suppose that that hon. Member has not had a wink of sleep since that time because of his embarrassment. No wonder the hon. Member for Bonavista-Twillingate suffered a minor breakdown in health, and I suppose that his medical adviser told him what caused his lack of sleep and probably suggested that we were responsible.
What did those hon. gentlemen try to do to Parliament? They tried to make it an institution which would bow to the use of blackmail. Does anyone think that such an attitude lends itself to the efficiency of Parliament? Le us consider the flag debate and how the Prime Minister somersaulted in that regard. He started out by suggesting that the issue should be non-partisan and that it should be sent to a committee. He then suggested that they were going to take this sacred symbol and use it for political purposes and the devil with Parliament and the
June I, 1965

people of Canada. That is, in fact, what the Government did. However, because the Opposition rose on its hind legs and said, no, you cannot do that, the Government turned to the people of Canada and suggested that we should change the rules to make sure that the time of Parliament was not wasted by the Opposition.
Surely that is the attitude obviously taken by the bunch over there on the front benches. It is true that the Prime Minister was finally beaten into changing his attitude to some extent, but by then he had done the harm to the country. By that time the Prime Minister had shown the people of this country that he did not care what happened, how long we worked, how bad our nerves became, or how inefficient Parliament became. Obviously he intended that we would not have a summer recess unless we submitted to his blackmail. Surely that is a terrible attitude for the Government to take in respect of Parliament, particularly when one considers that it is the duty of the Government to run the business of the country efficiently, to provide leadership in the House and to persuade hon. Members to accept certain measures.
It is obvious that the bunch now sitting on the front benches on the Government side cannot give effective leadership to Parliament. None of them has even bothered to consider or comment on whether the fact that we have five parties in the House has some bearing on the picture of Parliament as painted by a number of members of the press. I sometimes think it has. Certainly we have seen some parties in this House playing politics in a manner which defies description. They have made it plain that the Government can count on a majority, and this has taken away the Government's excuse for any untoward action which might be accounted for by any feeling of insecurity. Here is a party which can count on an absolute majority, a party which knows that whenever the chips are down there are certain groups which will abstain from voting or stand solidly with it, as the case may be, to make sure it is not defeated. Yet Members opposite still tell the nation: We must control Parliament; we do not have an absolute majority. They use that as an excuse.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I have not been in this House as long as some have been, but nothing can change my theory that Parliament exists to ensure that our democratic system works to the best
22620-119J
House of Commons Procedures advantage of the people of this country. One of the hard won rights of Parliament is the right to check Government excesses by ensuring that money is not granted until grievances have been redressed. Something within me quails when there is a suggestion that there should be limitation of debate when it comes to estimates and supply. I have not yet seen any necessity for such a limitation in this House. I have seen discussion continued right to the last day or two, yet somehow we have pushed through two or three departments; deals have been made. I am talking now about the days when this party formed the Government as well as the period when the Liberals formed the Government.
When the Liberals were in Opposition they said they had only one duty, to get rid of the Government. That was something entirely new to me. They regarded their duty as an Opposition to be no more than that. Taking an attitude such as this into account, and having regard to the kind of filibuster which went on among the Liberals and their supporters at that time, it is indeed surprising that supply was passed. But still supply was passed and the estimates were approved. When a Government cannot satisfy Parliament or redress the grievances of the House or when it cannot manage to get its legislation passed within a reasonable time, then one should look to the Government itself to discover the fault.
It is obvious from the remarks I have made, comparing this Government with the previous one, that I believe our rules must be applicable to normal parliamentary procedure over the long term. The situation arising in a two party House is different from that presented by a five party House. It is not reasonable, in my view, to say that as soon as the Government is in trouble Parliament is bad and we must therefore change the rules. No one has yet proved to my satisfaction that it is the rules which are to blame for the various troubles about which the Government complains. Nevertheless we have reached a frame of mind which has prompted many speakers to accept the desirability of change and concentrate their attention on what changes may be necessary to carry out reform. In doing this I believe we have reached a new low.
I would point out that the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) made it plain at the beginning of his speech that he was against any interference with the rights and, indeed,
June 1, 1985

House of Commons Procedures the duty of individual Members of Parliament to speak on behalf of their constituents. At the same time he thought we must limit debate. He found himself unable to come up with a practical solution to this dilemma. Those who have listened to other speeches will have found the same thread running through the debate. When Members begin talking about a solution before they have decided what has caused the trouble, when they say a change in the rules is needed in these circumstances, they run into difficulty with regard to the changes which should be made.
The truth is that most people are not sure what effect these changes will have. The difficulties inherent in these proposed changes have not been pointed out to them. Certainly some of us have vague notions of the factors which may have added to the inconvenience the House has suffered of late, but no evidence has been advanced as to the amount of trouble which our rules themselves have caused; no attempt has been made to indicate how much difficulty has been caused by our present procedure. There are many factors which enter into this. Whenever the Government is in trouble, Members opposite place the blame on the Opposition. Members opposite may not agree. What about the lack of leadership on the part of the Government? How big a factor is the presence of five parties? How large is the part played by the lack of restraint shown by some Members who show no regard at all for the rules? How big a factor is the obvious contempt for Parliament shown by the Liberals? When I talk about lack of restraint I confess that some hon. Members of my own party could show more restraint at times. The Creditistes should blush a little because in my opinion no group has bent the rules more than they have; they seem to feel they are misunderstood and that they alone possess rights.
We would all agree, I am sure, that a great deal more respect for the rules of this House would make the present rules more effective than they are now. I say to hon. Members: Let us all have a lot more respect for the rules. Let us all work harder together to try to make democracy work in this country. Then I defy anyone to tell me we need changes in our rules before we can get our work done in the manner in which it should be done. Respect for Parliament, the acknowledgement of the supremacy of the rules and respect for the work which has to be done

need leadership, and in the Parliament of Canada there is only one place where responsibility for leadership rests and that is on the shoulders of the Prime Minister and the cabinet he has chosen. As long as there is the contempt for Parliament this Government shows we shall have trouble carrying out the work of this House no matter how the rules are changed unless we want to fold up and become a complaisant rubber stamp, and I suggest this is the only reason the Government is putting forward these proposals now.
I thank the House for its attention. I only hope somebody on the Government side will get up and argue that we need these rule changes because so far we have not heard one bit of evidence to this effect.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

speechtext: May I ask the hon. Member the question I wished to ask him earlier? It is the same now, as it was at the beginning of his remarks. maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext: I suggest that Parliament, despite the abuse it has taken, despite the extra time Members have put in, has managed to get through the work it should have done and that it has worked well. All I can say is that, given the proper leadership, the proper guidance and the proper attitude toward Parliament, we might have done the same amount of work it took us ten months to do in six months or less.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to make my remarks strictly relevant to the amendment and subamendment before the House at the moment. I must admit frankly that I found it a little difficult to follow the argument of the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) when he suggested that someone was trying to make a rubber stamp of him. Somehow I could not quite visualize him in that role. I think he will not mind my making that remark. I think no one on our side would ever suggest that is a role that would fit him easily. As a matter of fact, I hope no one ever tries to put him in that position.
In so far as the amendment and subamendment are concerned, it seemed to me there were two rather unrelated questions linked up. The one had to do with a somewhat extraneous argument about whether or not the
June 1, 1965

leaders of the minorities or smaller groups in the House had rights that were different from those of individual private Members and what those rights should be. I do not propose to embark on that discussion because I think it is irrelevant to the particular point I want to make at this stage in the debate.
The other point was whether or not we should have, under the rules, an arbitrary restriction on the length of speeches made on any item of business that was before the House under an allocation of time. The proposal running through both the amendment and subamendment is that a time limit of 20 minutes should be put on a Member's speech, the same time on the Committee stage as would be allowed on second reading stage and third reading stage. I want to make it clear that the Government certainly is not asking for this kind of restriction on individual Members. If the individual Members feel there is something they need, I suggest that the remedy lies elsewhere than in that kind of amendment to the rules.
It is quite possible to visualize legislation of a nature that would perhaps have an allocation of time of two weeks at the second reading stage and several weeks in the Committee stage. I am thinking of legislation, for instance, like the medicare plan. I, for one, would very much dislike the proposition that under the rules we should fix arbitrarily a limit of 20 minutes on an individual Member's speech on the second reading of a bill of that scope. While I understand quite well the objective of hon. Members in moving the amendment and subamendment, I want to suggest, with all deference to them, that they may not have found an expression of the protection they desire in the proposal put before us.
I am going to suggest that the House consider that the allocation of time for individual speeches, provided it is going to be dealt with, is something that should vary from one item of business to another if there is to be any special provision at all made for it.
I had thought that the proposed new Standing Order as it now reads did provide this and that this was inherent in it. This view is not held by all hon. Members and it has been suggested that the proposed new rule dealing with allocation of time does not permit the Business Committee to deal with the allocation of time for speeches. If there is doubt on that point, and there seems to be-as a matter of fact, views quite firmly held indicate that the proposal does not contain that
House of Commons Procedures provision-I am quite prepared to move an amendment if the amendment and subamendment now before the House are withdrawn.
In order that hon. Members will understand what I am suggesting I propose to read an amendment, and if it appears to be satisfactory I think it would meet the situation. It would simply add subparagraph (9) to Standing Order 15A and would read something like this:
The term 'allocation of time', wherever used in this Standing Order may include the allotment of time to any item of business, to any stage thereof or any part thereof and may include the fixing of limits for the length of speeches.
The significant part is the fixing of limits for the length of speeches. There are other ways the point could be made by amending the Standing Order but the other ways, as I looked at them, involved amending several of the sections in this Standing Order. I think this is probably the simpler and better way of doing it. It does seem to me there conceivably may be a situation in which it is quite undesirable to limit the length of speeches on second reading stage but may be desirable to limit the length of speeches in Committee beyond the length now set by Standing Order. It may well be that on one item of business the House may wish no interference at all with the time limit on speeches that is now applicable, while on another piece of legislation the House might be agreeable to and indeed want quite a short period of time allocated. I am thinking of legislation upon which at the Committee stage the Members might want a short interval of time for individual speeches, perhaps as little as 10 minutes.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
In any event, it seems to me that this approach to the problem would more nearly meet the consensus of thinking there is in the House. Members, of course, have full protection when the matter has been dealt with by their representative on the Committee and, if there is an order to be made, when that is brought before the House. Therefore, with some uncertainty as to what the time should be, I certainly do not think that here and now we should try to put the House more or less in a strait-jacket for the next two years.
I should like to remind hon. Members that the Government offered an amendment to this proposal limiting its applicability to the balance of this session and one more session-
June 1, 1965

House of Commons Procedures It is not a permanent change, and I have no doubt that at the end of that period of time each one of us may have quite different ideas as to what might be done with the rules in one detail or another. I am quite sure experience will indicate certain changes, but I would prefer this more open method than the rigidity inherent in the amendment now.
Bearing that in mind, I wonder if the hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), who moved the subamendment, and the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), who moved the amendment and who regrettably is not here-though his party leader and house leader are-would consider the point I have made and let us know whether or not they are prepared to withdraw their amendments. If they are I would be prepared to move the amendment I have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to offer some comments in this debate. The Rules Committee which was set up some months ago did a great deal of work in connection with rule changes; weeks and months of consideration were given to this problem. Then when the House came to consider their recommendations it was found that, while they had brought forth some very worthwhile suggestions, those suggestions required further refining and the Government took it upon themselves to work out of the recommendations of the Committee on Rules proposals of their own for, as they say, bringing our House rules up to date.
I would agree with the suggestion of the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) that a clear case for a change in the rules has not been made. We have had our troubles in Parliament during the last two or three years. The hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) put at a 10-year period the time that Parliament has been destroying itself. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that most of the destruction has taken place inside the last three years. While I would hesitate to say it myself, I have noted that the hon. Member for Lapointe (Mr. Gre-goire) found that the difficulty with Parliament during these years has been the

DEBATES	June 1, 1965
methods which have been used by the one party in this House which has now assumed the responsibility of government. While they were in Opposition, and later when they took over the responsibility of government, they treated the House in such a way that a great deal of opposition and hostility was aroused. This fact has been noted by several Members during the course of their speeches, and it is up to everyone in the House to draw his own conclusions in that regard.
I should like to compliment the Committee on Rules for the work they put into that undertaking. I should even like to compliment the Government on their efforts to bring our rules up to date wherever possible.
I should like to make this point, however, that no single individual and no single authority created the rules of Parliament. They have grown over the years to fill a need, and in my opinion our forebears were just as wise as we are in the understanding of human nature; our forebears, our predecessors in this House, used the best intelligence they had in drawing up these rules. They are based on not only the experience of this Parliament; they are based on hundreds of years of experience in the Mother of Parliaments in Great Britain.
When we at this time set about reforming the rules and making drastic changes in the rules we are going to run into serious difficulty because the people who preceded us in this place gave careful thought to these rules -they must have-and they have been devised to protect and safeguard the rights of private Members in this House. When it has appeared that certain actions which should have been taken were not taken, there has been a reason for it. As this debate has gone forward I have noted greater and greater difficulties being drawn to the attention of the Government and the House in making any worth-while changes in the rules. We heard several speeches this afternoon, and I would refer to the speech of the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) who said he did not like to see any Member of this House prevented from making any speech which he felt it was necessary to make in the House.
e (9:10 p.m.)
We have heard the same sentiments expressed by the hon. Member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett). We cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. I think one of the points which our predecessors in this House observed and respected was that we must
June 1, 1965

put up with some inconvenience in this House if we are to have free speech on the part of the private Member.
The rights of the people's representatives to speak out in Parliament have been bought with the lives of men. These bulwarks of democracy have grown out of war and bloodshed. Our parliamentary safeguards have been baptized with blood. All our opposition should be applied to any suggestion to lay careless hands on these safeguards of democracy and toss them thoughtlessly into the discard. When we find widespread movement to reform this House, to bring in broad, comprehensive reforms, reforms which would change the nature of the place, then I say that any trend toward thoughtlessly tossing into the discard these blood-drenched rights which Parliaments have won through the years should be opposed with all that we have.
I propose to try to make the point that what is proposed here does in some respects do that very thing or tends toward that very thing. Far be it from me to suggest that our present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and our present Government would knowingly be guilty of any such conduct or would harbour any such thought. But I do say this, that we cannot be too careful to protect at all times these basic principles behind our right to speak out in this Parliament.
Years ago, when Parliament first began, the struggle was between Parliament and the Crown. My history teacher taught me that benevolent dictatorship, benevolent despotism, offered the finest form of Government known to man-the most efficient, the most kindly, the most just. But it came to light very early in history that dictatorship, despotism, could not be trusted. Despotic power in the hands of the right people was a great blessing but despotic power in the hands of the wrong people was a great curse.
Authority has now moved from the Crown to the Prime Minister and the Government. In these days with authority removed from the Crown there is no danger of despotism from that source. Today the danger of despotism comes from or lies with the Government of a democracy under a parliamentary system. Because a Prime Minister, the head of a democratic government, has more power in his hands than Kings have had, we need protection today against a Prime Minister under our parliamentary system of government, not against the Crown or against Parliament. For that reason care is needed in the protection of the safeguards which
House of Commons Procedures have been built into our parliamentary
system.
Government is an organized undertaking of all citizens to take care of each other, to provide for order and the protection of life, liberty and property. Nowadays it provides protection even against illness, death, privation and, of course, safeguards our freedom. As individuals we have very little power; it is only as we unite together and co-operate together that we have power. In essence, that is what our Government is, a co-operative effort on the part of all the citizens of the country to protect and care for each other. Civilization itself is the ability to co-operate; and Parliament is the centre of our national civilization.
No one created parliament or its parliamentary rules. Parliament and its rules grew to fill a need and grew out of the experience of the people. As I have already pointed out, it is not easy to improve the rules of Parliament. The rules which are now proposed might appear much safer if we had what those on the Government side call a continuing Speaker and what those on the Opposition side have called a permanent Speaker. If this step could be brought about it would make some of these proposed changes in our rules appear much safer that they appear at present.
I have been interested, Mr. Speaker, in the remarks which have been made by various speakers in this debate. I should like first to comment on a statement by the Prime Minister which intimated that he is well aware of the seriousness of these proposed rule changes. He speaks of the rule changes in Government Order 14 in this way, as reported at page 1474 of Hansard:
Together these two resolutions constitute, I believe, the most thorough proposals for the reform of the procedures of Parliament which have been considered by Parliament. And Parliament is our fundamental institution.
What we do with these proposals is therefore of great significance, I believe, for the future of our country, as it is for the working of our parliamentary institutions. In one sense it is domestic housekeeping, the amendment of our own rules, and it is being put forward as domestic housekeeping in no partisan way, because every Member of the House, whatever party he may represent, has his own interest in the rules of the House and its procedures. But while it may be domestic housekeeping in that sense, in another sense I believe we will be making a basic decision as to how Parliament shall do the business of the country. It is basic because, important as these resolutions are in themselves, this decision will also, I believe, be a point of departure in the conduct of parliamentary business and therefore in the operation of democracy itself.

must discipline ourselves.
Again I agree with the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona who pointed out that if we discipline ourselves to better advantage the work of this House is likely to be carried out much more smoothly and the image of Parliament now held by the people will be improved.
I should now like to comment briefly on some of the specific proposals outlined in this resolution. The second paragraph states:
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House-
In all kindness, Mr. Speaker, I think that should be modified to read: "That this House agrees upon the need for more fully allocating the time for the business of the House". The time of the House is now allocated. We have certain days for the Throne Speech debate, certain days for the budget debate and certain days are set aside for supply motions. We now have a great many allocations of times and, as a matter of fact, our rules relate mainly to the allocation of time. The second paragraph as now worded makes it appear that there has so far been no allocation of time. I think this is most unfair and I suggest to the Government that a word or words be added in this context before the word "allocated" so as to make this particular sentence nearer the truth.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I commend the Government on the changes which have been made, particularly in the provision that 30 days be allotted to the business of supply in each session. Again, I agree with the hon. Member for Edmonton Strath-cona (Mr. Nugent) that this could be very useful, though I doubt whether it is necessary. However, I would be quite prepared to go along with it on the trial basis which is suggested. The supplementary estimates which are introduced subsequent to the main estimates are excluded from the 30 day provision and I think this represents a great improvement.
The number of supply motions is to be reduced from six to four. This will save us four days during a session. I think we have plenty of opportunities to test the Government in these votes in which confidence is involved. There are opportunities during debate on the address and further opportunities during the budget debate. I should like to raise a question in connection with the provision set out here in 1(c):

House of Commons Procedures
That a Special Committee of the House consisting of 24 Members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consquential upon these orders, including any means of giving to the Opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
I should like to see that last clause made mandatory rather than permissive. It could be worded to read as follows:
-consequential upon these orders which shall include some means of giving to the Opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
We should make it clear there is no question about it; the Opposition shall have opportunities to select the departmental estimates to be brought up for discussion.
As far as I am concerned, each of these recommendations is acceptable. Clause 5 does, I think, contain a danger but as long as it is to be introduced on a trial basis it is not such a strain to accept. Clause 7 making provision for a minimum number of days for committee stage discussions and so on, appears to be a good idea. Clause 8, which allows the Speaker to add extra days for discussion when unexpected amendments are moved to legislation, also appears to offer a useful safeguard. Again, the proposal that the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order and the new Standing Order 15A be continued in effect to the end of the next ensuing session unless the House otherwise orders, makes acceptance tolerable.
I have already commented on the suggestion that there be a continuing or permanent Speaker. There is the matter of the question period. I have felt that the question period has been much misused. It seems to me that we could have a question period as effective as it is at present while possibly saving a great deal of time if we could make some changes in this regard. I do not know whether this would be practicable but I make this suggestion for what it is worth, that a limitation be placed on the number of questions or subjects which could be raised during any question period on any day. As a basis for discussion I would suggest four per day for the Official Opposition, one per day for the Government and one each for the three smaller parties. These could be distributed so that everyone in the parties would have a chance. Supplementary questions arising out of these basic questions might be open to anyone, limited only by the Speaker in the exercise of his discretion. Such an arrangement might have the effect of limiting the number of subjects raised without curtailing

I believe that the provisions of clause 5 in part 3 constitute closure and the only ground upon which I can accept this is that it is being introduced on a trial basis. Maybe it should not be accepted in any circumstances.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There is the question of committee work. A number of complaints have been made that after committees have given consideration to the various matters referred to them and have drawn up reports which often contain valuable suggestions, the reports are ignored and are never heard of again. The House is never given a chance to discuss these recommendations and reports. I believe that when the new rules are drawn up provision should be made for bringing these reports before the House. During the course of the debate, a statement could be made by a Minister or the Minister concerned indicating the attitude of the Government toward the recommendation to which the Committee had given a great deal of consideration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the House any longer. I appreciate very much this opportunity to make these comments and I hope this effort to amend the rules will prove successful and help us in making the House more effective in the handling of our nation's business.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for just a few minutes, and in doing so I am. of course, exercising my right to speak while the subamendment of the hon. However, I am really rising to respond to the suggestion that was made earlier by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) when he indicated that if the amendment and subamendment now before the House were withdrawn, someone on the Government side would move as an amendment the new paragraph 9 to Standing Order 15A, the terms of which he read to the House the last time he was on his feet.
It is becoming quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has raised an important point and one that Members in many quarters of the House feel should be considered. I should like to say, on behalf of the Member for Greenwood, that he was not endeavouring to bring in through the back door some extraneous

DEBATES	June 1, 1965
principles. If some things seem to have been brought in, one will just have to take it that way. His main concern, which I thought he stated quite effectively in his speech last Thursday night, is a very simple one, namely, that if a time limit is to be placed on the length of a debate itself, surely it makes sense to look at the amount of time allotted to individual speakers within that total time limit.
I recognize the point made by the President of the Privy Council and others that one must not be too rigid about a matter of this kind. It may well be that one wants a different time limit in Committee of the Whole from the time limit that might be appropriate at second reading stage. I would admit also that a debate that is under a total time allocation of five days presents a different story from a debate that is under a time allocation of 10 or 15 days. For these reasons there obviously is some merit to the proposal made by the President of the Privy Council, namely, that instead of writing the actual number of minutes to be allotted to each speaker into Standing Order 15A, the Business Committee could be given authority to recommend to the House the fixing of a limit for the length of speeches.
As hon. Members are aware, indeed the President of the Privy Council referred to the fact a moment ago, the hon. Member for Greenwood is away. He had to leave last night for Belgrade, Yugoslavia, for a meeting of an international conference he is attending. However, before he left, lawyer that he is, he gave me his power of attorney to deal with this resolution.

The point I am really concerned about is that which was raised by the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) regarding the individual private Member in the House and his right to speak. Under our present scheme of things any Member, no matter whether he is in good faith or bad with his party, can get up and speak on legislation because if the Whip of his party has submitted a list of speakers and that list is exhausted the individual Member concerned can then stand up and will be recognized by Mr. Speaker. Normally we do not reach that sort of situation because party discipline and co-operation between party Members are such that there is agreement on who should appear on the Whip's list. Nevertheless a member who feels strongly and who is unable to convince his party that he should speak has a basic right to speak as a Member of the House, and a Member who is going to exercise that right under those conditions I would think would be one who would want to take a position different from that of his party.
This right is one that should not be lightly removed. If we proceed to allocation of time for both estimates and legislation this right of a private Member may disappear, and while it is not likely that this is going to happen it is still possible for a Member to be excluded from speaking by his party merely refusing to put him on the list that is submitted to the Speaker. I am very concerned about this fundamental right of a Member to disagree with his own party. It is something we should not throw away lightly, and I suggest that to get around this we could make a change in clause 7 which at present has the following words:
-provided it is continued, it necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak.
I suggest we change those words and replace them with the following:
-provided that if any Member of a party desires to speak who has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended but not later than the beginning of the next sitting day, until each such Member has had an opportunity to speak.
I know people will say that under this provision we might have to sit all night. I do not think we would have to, because this sort of provision would only apply in the very rare instance where normal party discipline and normal party co-operation have

DEBATES	June I, 1865
broken down. It seems to me that under those circumstances, that is the very time when it is worth sitting 15 or 20 minutes extra to hear one Member who feels strongly enough that possibly he wants to go against his own party and get his views on record.
I would hope consideration might be given to this sort of solution to the problem that has been raised. I believe it is a serious problem. I believe the right that is being removed is one that should not lightly be removed and I would hope we could find an answer such as this to effect a compromise between reasonable limitation of debate on the one hand and the right, on the other hand, of a Member who feels strongly to get up and say his piece.

That Standing Order 15 be amended by adding thereto, immediately after sub-order (2) thereof, the following:
"(2-a) In every Parliament as necessity may arise under the orders, usages and customs of the House, Mr. Speaker shall recognize the Prime Minister and the Member occupying the recognized position of the Leader of the Opposition, the Member speaking for the Prime Minister, or the Member speaking for the Leader of the Opposition, and no other."
I support the subamendment because I believe that our whole difficulty, as I have
June 1, 1965	COMMONS
said on previous occasions, is the proliferation of parties in the House. I believe everyone will agree that the institution in which we sit this evening was constituted for the hearing of the two sides of each argument. There may be differing views in the introduction of a piece of legislation and there may be differing views in opposing it, but surely to goodness just because certain areas of the country wish to elect one group or another that does not mean to say that particular group has a special place in opposition or special status as individuals. maintopic: PUBLIC WORKS-LAKE ONTARIO-PERMISSION FOR DUMPING OF FILL
PUBLIC WORKS-LAKE ONTARIO-PERMISSION FOR DUMPING OF FILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank some of the recent speakers this evening for their references to myself. I should like to take the next seven minutes to make some comments with regard to the action of the Government in respect of land fill in Lake Ontario, and in so doing I may indicate a somewhat independent approach to the question, if not on a party line.
I was forced on Thursday of last week to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) this question:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Can the Minister advise this House whether every individual or company that has dumped thousands of tons of fill into Lake Ontario between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek in the past few years received permission in advance, as required by the Navigable Waters Protection Act?
This question was forced upon the Minister of Public Works because of the ceaseless activity that is going on on the north shore of Lake Ontario in the vicinity of the City
DEBATES	1865
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of Toronto in the matter of filling in the shore line of Lake Ontario. There are plans afoot in our metropolitan area at the present time to build a tremendous park immediately south of Scarborough using sanitary fill or sanitary waste to make the base. This is to be covered later with good earth and a park developed.
There is a plan afoot to build 600 acres out into Lake Ontario immediately south of the Exhibition grounds, which would be bigger than the present area of Toronto Island. It is estimated that this proposed waterfront land change will take 22 million tons of waste and earth, and the total area of the filled project will be greater than the area of Toronto Island. From the Humber River over to Etobicoke Creek, a distance of four miles, which is the frontage of Lake Ontario of the ridings of York-Humber and York West, there have been tens of thousands of tons of fill dumped into the lake in the past few years.
I have asked when the Government is going to enforce the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which is still in effect in this country but evidently not enforced by anyone. In that regard I read to you section 4 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless
(a)	the site and plans thereof have been approved by the Minister: and
(b)	the work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations.
Down opposite the Village of Long Branch there has been a water lot filled with solid earth and it is projecting out of the water now about nine feet. I have in my hand a letter from the Department of Public Works:
This Department has not granted Millgate Park Investments-
This is the company that has filled in the water lot.
-authority to fill in a section of the shore line of Lake Ontario at or near Long Branch.
The Navigable Waters Protection Act goes on to state what the penalty will be if land fill is placed on the shore line of a navigable water without the prior consent of the Department of Public Works. It says:
Any work to which this Part applies that is built or placed upon a site not approved by the Minister, or is not built or placed in accordance with plans so approved, or, having been so built or placed, is not maintained in accordance with such plans and the regulations, may be removed and destroyed by the Minister-
June 1, 1365
1866	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
You will note that it says "may be removed and destroyed by the Minister". No action whatsoever has been taken. A letter dated January 21 was sent to Millgate Park Investments telling them that they must stop the fill, and it was very conveniently lost by the company and not found until March 4, by which time the fill had been completed. The municipal authorities in the Village of Long Branch are quite anxious to secure tax revenue by taxing this newly made earth, which I maintain, as do other observers, is completely illegal; it should not have been built without the prior consent of the Department of Public Works. But we find that the Long Branch Planning Board Chairman, at the meeting at which the rezoning of the lot was approved, said:
Legality is of interest, but has no direct connection with us.
At the same time, the Reeve of Long Branch, Tom Berry, also stated that legality may be of interest. He said:
-the legal implications are only secondary questions-
On the 23rd day of March, which is 10 weeks ago today, I asked the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) if he would advise me whether the International Joint Commission had given authority to dump fill into Lake Ontario and was told that the matter would be studied. They are still studying it. A couple of weeks ago I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) if he would define for us, or ask the Supreme Court of Canada to define, several words in the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act, and he also told us it would be studied and was a matter of great interest. Nothing is done, and yet there are three departments of Government that are vitally interested in this matter. I have a letter signed by a Member of the Cabinet which says that the sole interest of the Federal Government in this problem is related to the responsibility assumed under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I should like to state that there is another interest of the Federal Government, and I hope that the Cabinet Minister concerned will realize it. It is covered by the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act, which says that if the level of the lake is materially affected the two Governments have to come to agreement as to the work being done. I would ask the Minister of Public Works whether he will give us a table and check the dates on which prior authority was granted for the filling in of the shoreline by various landowners


from the Humber River to Etobicoke Creek during the past few years. The Ontario Hydro, living up to the letter of the law, secured permission to build their long wharf outside the coal electricity generating station south of Toronto Township in Peel County. If the Department of Public Works gave permission to the Hydro to build the wharf and to do this legally and properly, why was not the Navigable Waters Protection Act enforced with regard to all the earth which has been dumped into Lake Ontario between the Humber River and that legally erected wharf belonging to the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission?

maintopic: PUBLIC WORKS-LAKE ONTARIO-PERMISSION FOR DUMPING OF FILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of the hon. Member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) was raised during the oral question period last Thursday. He asked whether the Minister could advise the House if any individual or company which has dumped thousands of tons of fill into Lake Ontario between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek in the past few years received permission in advance as required by the Navigable Waters Protection Act. The short answer to this question is no, Mr. Speaker.
It is the opinion of officials of the Department of Public Works that the fill placed in this area to date is not substantially interfering with commercial navigation. The responsibility of the Department is to see that fill is properly contained and not allowed to erode. Interested home owners along the lake front have shown concern and have made efforts to stop the erection of proposed buildings. So far these home owners have not been successful and they are exploring other legal means to bring about the desired result. The hon. Member for York West (Mr. Kelly) as well as the hon. Member for York-Humber have made representations on behalf of home owners about this situation.
On January 1 of this year the Department requested Millgate Park Investments Limited to take steps to contain the fill dumped on their shore property at Long Branch to prevent erosion and also requested that lights be installed on the outer end of the fill. The Millgate firm advised the Department that

it was seeking permission from the Village of Long Branch to erect an apartment building and until permission was granted and the type of building approved the firm was not in a position to state the type of retaining wall that would be required.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday and Thursday of last week, as recorded at pages 1617 and 1714 of Hansard, I asked questions regarding the Canadian Assistance Plan. My questions were based on speeches made recently by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, notably one made at Charlottetown on May 20, in which she emphasized the fact that under the Canada Assistance Plan it will be possible for recipients of old age security to draw something more than the $75 they are now receiving. The question I put to the Government was quite straightforward.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In view of the emphasis being placed on what will be available to old age security recipients under the Canada Assistance Plan, will steps be taken to get this legislation before Parliament at an early date? Last Tuesday the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) replied to the effect that my question would be looked at and studied. The reply made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) last Thursday was the old one, that this has to be studied jointly by the Federal Government and the provinces.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, hundreds of thousands of people across this country, whose only income is the $75 per month which they receive under old age security, are waiting for some means by which they can obtain an increase in that pension benefit. This House and the country knows that we favour increasing the old age security pension to $100 per month. I have a resolution on the order paper to that effect. We in this party moved all the amendments we could in an attempt to bring this about when the Canada Pension Plan was under consideration during the last session. It is my firm belief that the time will come and that it is not too far away when we will have to raise the old age security pension to $100 a month.
In the meantime the Government shows no sign of moving in this direction but rather
DEBATES	1867
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion suggests that the Canada Assistance Plan is the answer and that the Canada Assistance Plan is legislation under which, on a needs test rather than on a means test, people on old age security will be able to obtain an additional benefit.
If the Minister and other Members of the Government are going to go about the country holding out this hope to the people, the Government is duty bound to bring this legislation before Parliament and get it on the statute books. The Minister has no right to go about the country making speeches of this kind, holding out this kind of promise, unless the Government means business.
It seems to me that we are right back where we were with the Canada Pension Plan, that piece of legislation which I think Parliament did a good job in passing but which took months of pulling to get it on the Order Paper, months of argument to get it before the House and finally to get it on the statute books. I hope we are not going to experience that same number of months and that same number of revisions with respect to the Canada Assistance Plan. If it is a good piece of legislation, as the Prime Minister said it was when he spoke about it on April 6, and if it is a good piece of legislation, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare says it is, let us at least get it on the order paper, let us at least have the details and let us see whether Parliament is willing, as I believe it will be, to expedite its passage.
We are improving our rules of procedure- at least I hope we are-with the measures now before the House of Commons. When we complete these measures we will have time to deal with the Canada Assistance Plan, and medicare too, and in the name of the people of Canada I urge the Government to put this piece of legislation on the order paper at the earliest possible date.
As I have stated, the Minister has no right to hold out the promise that here is more money for our old age security pensioners unless the Government means business. In view of the fact that the Government has said, through the Minister, that this extra money will be made available to pensioners under the Canada Assistance Plan, the Government is duty bound to bring this legislation before Parliament at the earliest possible date, and I hope tonight I will be able to get from the Parliamentary Secretary a more definite answer to my question than was given last week by either the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: CANADA ASSISTANCE PLAN-REQUEST FOR EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre strikes me as one of his more political speeches, particularly when he refers to the Canada Pension Plan as being the result, and I think his inference was undeniable, of the pushing and urging, I take it, of himself. As the hon. Member well knows, the Canada Pension Plan was undertaken by the Government within a month of its taking office. As a result of a series of meetings with provincial premiers, who have a fair amount of jurisdiction in this field, difficulties arose. I think this will always be the case in Canada. It was only after considerable negotiations at provincial levels that something was worked out. It certainly received the full attention of the top officials of the Department of Welfare. I believe the hon. Member well knows that this is the case.
As far as the Canada Assistance Plan is concerned it would be inaccurate to leave the impression that it is not receiving top priority attention and is not receiving the Government's attention at the present time. We have just dealt with certain substantial amendments to the Old Age Security Act raising old age security benefits, tying them to the cost of living and lowering the age qualification, and then the implementation of the Canada Pension Plan. For over a year the
Department has been turning its attention to the Canada Assistance Plan trying to work out with the Provinces a system for its implementation. This question was discussed in May, 1964, and there were further discussions leading to the meetings of welfare ministers on April 8 and 9 of this year when a general consensus was reached as to principle. This will involve a further discussion at the Federal-Provincial conference to be held shortly, as the hon. gentleman knows.
I anticipate that loose ends will be tied up at a further meeting of welfare ministers in the autumn. All these meetings are essential in connection with any project which requires agreement with all the provinces. We must go through this procedure. At the same time as the work of the officials is going on, draft legislation is being prepared.
